With vaccinations and policy support, the FOMC judged that economic activity and employment continued to improve and kept the federal funds rate at 0–0.25% while beginning a gradual taper of asset purchases. Inflation was elevated but seen as largely transitory, and the Committee emphasized that risks to the outlook persisted.

Incorporating SLOOS insights tilts the tone more positive on credit supply and demand than previously assessed. Banks broadly eased lending standards across residential real estate (including jumbo/QM and HELOCs), multifamily and nonfarm nonresidential CRE, and consumer credit (credit cards and autos). Lenders increased credit limits on credit cards and reduced auto rates, and they expected stronger demand for C&I and credit card loans; consumer loan demand was reported stronger. Foreign banks reported stronger demand for CRE and eased CRE standards, citing improved economic outlook, competition, greater risk tolerance, and strong liquidity/capital positions. Offsetting factors include pockets of weaker demand in auto and some C&I segments and unchanged standards for certain government mortgage categories. Net, SLOOS points to accommodative credit conditions that reinforce the FOMC’s view that financial conditions remain supportive, modestly improving the overall assessment despite financial stability vulnerabilities highlighted elsewhere.

Given these SLOOS signals of easier bank credit and firmer demand, the overall tone moves from moderately positive but tempered to somewhat more positive while still cautious.
